name: Methane burns
player_sees: flame: blue; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.1 'Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations'
claim_or_entries: Gives CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O.

name: Hydrogen burns
player_sees: flame: almost invisible pale blue; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Hydrogen'
claim_or_entries: Gives 2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l); hydrogen flames emit faint blue light and are nearly invisible in daylight.

name: Water splits
player_sees: gas H2; gas O2; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Electrolysis of water'
claim_or_entries: Gives 2H2O -> 2H2(g) + O2(g), hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode; standard enthalpy change +285.83 kJ per mole of water.

name: Charcoal burns
player_sees: glows; gas CO2; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Combustion'
claim_or_entries: 'Carbon will yield carbon dioxide' when burned completely.
note: The page states it in words; the equation is not printed.

name: Iron rusts
player_sees: Fe(s) grey goes; Fe2O3(s) red-brown appears; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Rust'
claim_or_entries: 'When iron is in contact with water and oxygen, it rusts'; rust is hydrous iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3.nH2O, usually reddish-brown.
note: Simplified: the game writes anhydrous Fe2O3 and leaves the water of the hydrate out. The page does not state the heat; the heat direction is from CRC enthalpies of formation.

name: Baking soda meets vinegar
player_sees: gas CO2; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Sodium bicarbonate'
claim_or_entries: Gives NaHCO3 + CH3COOH -> CH3COONa + H2O + CO2(g).
note: That it takes in heat is from CRC enthalpies of formation (+31 kJ), not from the page.

name: Photosynthesis
player_sees: gas O2; note: In pondweed, small bubbles of oxygen rise from the leaves in light; takes in heat
source: OpenStax, Biology 2e (2018), section 8.1 'Overview of Photosynthesis', Figure 8.5
claim_or_entries: Figure 8.5: 'six carbon dioxide and six water molecules produce one sugar molecule and six oxygen molecules', using light energy.

name: Respiration
player_sees: gas CO2; note: Happens all the time inside living cells: nothing to see in a flask; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Cellular respiration'
claim_or_entries: Gives C6H12O6(s) + 6O2(g) -> 6CO2(g) + 6H2O(l) + energy, in steps run by enzymes.

name: A candle burns
player_sees: flame: luminous yellow; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Paraffin wax'
claim_or_entries: Paraffin wax is a mixture of alkanes with 20 to 40 carbon atoms, used for candles; Wikipedia 'Alkane' gives complete combustion of any alkane to CO2 and H2O.
note: C25H52 stands for the mixture; the page names C31H64 as a typical component, not C25H52.

name: Hydrogen peroxide splits
player_sees: gas O2; note: With a catalyst, the liquid froths with oxygen; gives off heat
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2 'Classifying Chemical Reactions'
claim_or_entries: Example 4.6: 2H2O2(aq) -> 2H2O(l) + O2(g).

name: Magnesium burns
player_sees: flame: brilliant white; glows; Mg(s) silvery goes; MgO(s) white appears; smoke of MgO (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Magnesium'
claim_or_entries: 'The free metal burns with a brilliant-white light'; with air or oxygen it forms only the oxide MgO.

name: Propane burns
player_sees: flame: blue; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Propane'
claim_or_entries: 'In the presence of excess oxygen, propane burns to form water and carbon dioxide.'
note: The page does not state the flame colour shown (blue).

name: Ethanol burns
player_sees: flame: pale blue; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ethanol'
claim_or_entries: Gives C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l); 'it burns with a smokeless blue flame that is not always visible in normal light'.

name: Yeast ferments sugar
player_sees: gas CO2; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ethanol fermentation'
claim_or_entries: Gives C6H12O6 + 2ADP + 2Pi -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 + 2ATP; yeasts do it without oxygen, with enzymes.
note: The game leaves out ADP and ATP.

name: Limewater turns milky
player_sees: solid CaCO3 (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Limewater'
claim_or_entries: Gives Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l); 'the solution takes on a milky appearance'.

name: Sodium meets water
player_sees: gas H2; note: The sodium melts into a fizzing silvery ball that skates on the water; gives off heat
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.1 'Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations'
claim_or_entries: Gives 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g); Wikipedia 'Alkali metal': all alkali metals melt as they react with water.

name: Lithium meets water
player_sees: gas H2; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkali metal'
claim_or_entries: Alkali metals react with cold water to give the hydroxide and hydrogen; 'lithium reacts steadily with effervescence'.
note: The page states the general reaction, not this equation.

name: Potassium meets water
player_sees: flame: lilac; gas H2; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkali metal'
claim_or_entries: Alkali metals react with cold water to give the hydroxide and hydrogen; sodium and potassium can ignite; potassium's flame-test colour is violet (Wikipedia 'Flame test': lilac).
note: The page states the general reaction, not this equation.

name: Calcium meets water
player_sees: gas H2; solid Ca(OH)2 (white); Ca(s) silvery grey goes; Ca(OH)2(s) white appears; note: Calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble, so the water turns cloudy white; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkaline earth metal'
claim_or_entries: 'Calcium, strontium, and barium react with water to produce hydrogen gas and their respective hydroxides.'

name: Barium meets water
player_sees: gas H2; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkaline earth metal'
claim_or_entries: 'Calcium, strontium, and barium react with water to produce hydrogen gas and their respective hydroxides.'

name: Strontium meets water
player_sees: gas H2; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkaline earth metal'
claim_or_entries: 'Calcium, strontium, and barium react with water to produce hydrogen gas and their respective hydroxides.'

name: Magnesium meets steam
player_sees: flame: brilliant white; gas H2; Mg(s) silvery goes; MgO(s) white appears; smoke of MgO (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Magnesium'
claim_or_entries: With steam, magnesium produces magnesium oxide and hydrogen.

name: Sodium meets chlorine
player_sees: flame: yellow-orange; Na(s) silvery goes; Cl2(g) pale yellow-green goes; NaCl(s) white appears; smoke of NaCl (white); gives off heat
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2 'Classifying Chemical Reactions'
claim_or_entries: Gives 2Na(s) + Cl2(g) -> 2NaCl(s); Wikipedia 'Halogen': heated sodium reacts with halogens with bright-orange flames.

name: Potassium meets chlorine
player_sees: flame: lilac; K(s) silvery goes; Cl2(g) pale yellow-green goes; KCl(s) white appears; smoke of KCl (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkali metal'
claim_or_entries: Alkali metals 'react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides'.
note: General statement; the equation is not printed.

name: Magnesium meets chlorine
player_sees: flame: brilliant white; Mg(s) silvery goes; Cl2(g) pale yellow-green goes; MgCl2(s) white appears; smoke of MgCl2 (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkaline earth metal'
claim_or_entries: All the alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form halides (example Ca + Cl2 -> CaCl2).
note: General statement; the magnesium equation is not printed.

name: Calcium meets chlorine
player_sees: flame: orange-red; Ca(s) silvery grey goes; Cl2(g) pale yellow-green goes; CaCl2(s) white appears; smoke of CaCl2 (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkaline earth metal'
claim_or_entries: Gives Ca + Cl2 -> CaCl2.

name: Aluminium meets chlorine
player_sees: glows; Al(s) silvery goes; Cl2(g) pale yellow-green goes; AlCl3(s) white to pale yellow appears; smoke of AlCl3 (white to pale yellow); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Aluminium chloride'
claim_or_entries: Made 'by the exothermic reaction of aluminium metal with chlorine', 2Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3; anhydrous AlCl3 is colourless, often yellow from iron(III) chloride.

name: Copper meets chlorine
player_sees: glows; Cu(s) pink-brown goes; Cl2(g) pale yellow-green goes; CuCl2(s) yellow-brown appears; smoke of CuCl2 (yellow-brown); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Copper(II) chloride'
claim_or_entries: 'Copper at red heat ... combines directly with chlorine gas, giving (molten) copper(II) chloride'; the anhydrous form is dark brown.
note: The game shows anhydrous CuCl2 as yellow-brown.

name: Sodium meets bromine
player_sees: Na(s) silvery goes; Br2(l) deep red-brown goes; NaBr(s) white appears; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkali metal'
claim_or_entries: Alkali metals 'react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides'; Wikipedia 'Halogen': heated sodium reacts with halogens with bright-orange flames.
note: General statement. The game shows no flame for this one (for review).

name: Iron meets sulfur
player_sees: glows; Fe(s) grey goes; S(s) bright yellow goes; FeS(s) black appears; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Iron(II) sulfide'
claim_or_entries: 'FeS can be obtained by the heating of iron and sulfur', Fe + S -> FeS; iron sulfides are black.

name: Magnesium meets sulfur
player_sees: flame: brilliant white; Mg(s) silvery goes; S(s) bright yellow goes; MgS(s) white appears; smoke of MgS (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Magnesium sulfide'
claim_or_entries: 'MgS is formed by the reaction of sulfur or hydrogen sulfide with magnesium'; white, often brown when impure.

name: Copper turns black
player_sees: Cu(s) pink-brown goes; CuO(s) black appears; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Copper(II) oxide'
claim_or_entries: 'It can be formed by heating copper in air at around 300-800 C', 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO; a black solid.

name: Zinc burns
player_sees: flame: bluish-green; Zn(s) bluish grey goes; ZnO(s) white appears; smoke of ZnO (white); note: Zinc oxide is yellow while hot and turns white as it cools; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Zinc oxide'
claim_or_entries: Zinc vapour reacts with the oxygen of air to give ZnO with bright luminescence (French process); ZnO is yellow when hot and white when cold.
note: The flame colour shown (bluish-green) is not on the page.

name: Aluminium oxidises
player_sees: flame: brilliant white; Al(s) silvery goes; Al2O3(s) white appears; smoke of Al2O3 (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Aluminium'
claim_or_entries: Aluminium forms one stable oxide, Al2O3; 'a fine powder of aluminium reacts explosively on contact with liquid oxygen'.
note: The page does not describe aluminium powder burning in air or its brilliant white flame.

name: Lithium burns
player_sees: flame: crimson; Li(s) silvery goes; Li2O(s) white appears; smoke of Li2O (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Lithium oxide'
claim_or_entries: Lithium burns in air: 4Li + O2 -> 2Li2O; Wikipedia 'Flame test': lithium colours a flame carmine red.

name: Sodium tarnishes
player_sees: Na(s) silvery goes; Na2O(s) white appears; note: The shiny cut surface goes dull white within seconds as oxide forms. Sodium only bursts into a yellow-orange flame when it is heated; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Sodium oxide'
claim_or_entries: Gives 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O (burning in air gives a mixture with sodium peroxide).
note: At room temperature the cut surface tarnishes; the peroxide is left out.

name: Calcium burns
player_sees: flame: orange-red; Ca(s) silvery grey goes; CaO(s) white appears; smoke of CaO (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkaline earth metal'
claim_or_entries: Gives 2Ca + O2 -> 2CaO; Wikipedia 'Flame test': calcium colours a flame brick or orange red.

name: Silicon burns
player_sees: glows; Si(s) shiny grey goes; SiO2(s) white appears; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Silicon dioxide'
claim_or_entries: Dry oxidation at 600-1200 C: Si + O2 -> SiO2.

name: Sulfur burns
player_sees: flame: blue; gas SO2; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Sulfur dioxide'
claim_or_entries: Burning sulfur: S8 + 8O2 -> 8SO2, dH = -297 kJ/mol.
note: The blue flame shown is not on the page.

name: Phosphorus burns
player_sees: flame: bright yellow-white; P4(s) waxy pale yellow goes; P4O10(s) white appears; smoke of P4O10 (white); gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Phosphorus pentoxide'
claim_or_entries: 'P4O10 is prepared by burning white phosphorus with a sufficient supply of oxygen', P4 + 5O2 -> P4O10.

name: Carbon monoxide burns
player_sees: flame: blue; gas CO2; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Carbon monoxide'
claim_or_entries: CO 'burns with a blue flame, producing carbon dioxide'.

name: Carbon burns with little air
player_sees: glows; gas CO; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Carbon monoxide'
claim_or_entries: Made 'by the direct oxidation of carbon in a limited supply of oxygen or air', 2C + O2 -> 2CO.

name: Ethane burns
player_sees: flame: blue; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.1 'Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations'
claim_or_entries: Gives 2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 6H2O + 4CO2.

name: Butane burns
player_sees: flame: blue; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkane'
claim_or_entries: Complete combustion of any alkane: CnH2n+2 + (3n+1)/2 O2 -> (n+1)H2O + nCO2.
note: General equation applied with n = 4.

name: Pentane burns
player_sees: flame: luminous yellow; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkane'
claim_or_entries: Complete combustion of any alkane: CnH2n+2 + (3n+1)/2 O2 -> (n+1)H2O + nCO2.
note: General equation applied with n = 5.

name: Hexane burns
player_sees: flame: luminous yellow; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkane'
claim_or_entries: Complete combustion of any alkane: CnH2n+2 + (3n+1)/2 O2 -> (n+1)H2O + nCO2.
note: General equation applied with n = 6.

name: Petrol burns
player_sees: flame: luminous yellow; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Alkane'
claim_or_entries: Complete combustion of any alkane: CnH2n+2 + (3n+1)/2 O2 -> (n+1)H2O + nCO2.
note: General equation applied with n = 8.

name: Ethene burns
player_sees: flame: luminous yellow; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2 'Classifying Chemical Reactions'
claim_or_entries: Example 4.6: C2H4(g) + 3O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(l) (combustion).
note: The luminous yellow flame shown is not on the page.

name: Acetylene burns
player_sees: flame: luminous yellow; gas CO2; gas H2O; smoke (black soot); condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Combustion'
claim_or_entries: 'When a hydrocarbon burns in oxygen, the reaction will primarily yield carbon dioxide and water'; Wikipedia 'Acetylene': its combustion gives a strong, bright light.
note: General statement; the sooty flame shown is not on the page.

name: Benzene burns
player_sees: flame: luminous yellow; gas CO2; gas H2O; smoke (black soot); condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Combustion'
claim_or_entries: 'When a hydrocarbon burns in oxygen, the reaction will primarily yield carbon dioxide and water'; Wikipedia 'Benzene' gives its enthalpy of combustion, -3267.6 kJ/mol.
note: General statement; the sooty flame shown is not on the page.

name: Methanol burns
player_sees: flame: pale blue; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Methanol'
claim_or_entries: Gives 2CH3OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 4H2O; 'methanol flames are invisible in daylight'.

name: Propanol burns
player_sees: flame: pale blue; gas CO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, '1-Propanol'
claim_or_entries: A flammable liquid with a standard enthalpy of combustion of -2021 kJ/mol (which is defined for burning to CO2 and H2O).
note: The page does not print the equation or describe the flame.

name: Ammonia burns in oxygen
player_sees: flame: pale yellowish-green; gas N2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ammonia'
claim_or_entries: Mixed with oxygen it 'burns with a pale yellowish-green flame', 4NH3 + 3O2 -> 2N2 + 6H2O(g).

name: Hydrogen sulfide burns
player_sees: flame: blue; gas SO2; gas H2O; condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Hydrogen sulfide'
claim_or_entries: It 'burns in oxygen with a blue flame to form sulfur dioxide and water', 2H2S + 3O2 -> 2SO2 + 2H2O.

name: Carbon disulfide burns
player_sees: flame: blue; gas CO2; gas SO2; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Carbon disulfide'
claim_or_entries: Gives CS2 + 3O2 -> CO2 + 2SO2.
note: The blue flame shown is not on the page.

name: Silane catches fire
player_sees: flame: not recorded here; gas H2O; smoke of SiO2 (white); condensation; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Silane'
claim_or_entries: Silane is pyrophoric; SiH4 + 2O2 -> SiO2 + 2H2O.

name: Haber process
player_sees: gas NH3; note: Nothing to see: colourless gases in a steel reactor; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Haber process'
claim_or_entries: N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, an exothermic equilibrium, over finely divided iron at 150-250 bar and 450-550 C.

name: Ammonia cracks
player_sees: gas N2; gas H2; note: Nothing to see: colourless gases; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ammonia'
claim_or_entries: 'At high temperature and in the presence of a suitable catalyst, ammonia decomposes into its constituent elements'; slightly endothermic.

name: Hydrogen meets chlorine
player_sees: gas HCl; Cl2(g) pale yellow-green goes; note: In bright light the mixture explodes; the yellow-green colour vanishes; gives off heat
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2 'Classifying Chemical Reactions'
claim_or_entries: Gives H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g); Wikipedia 'Halogen': explosive in the presence of light.

name: Hydrogen meets bromine
player_sees: gas HBr; Br2(g) red-brown goes; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Bromine'
claim_or_entries: HBr is made by 'the reaction of hydrogen gas with bromine gas at 200-400 C with a platinum catalyst'.
note: The game asks for heat only; the page names a platinum catalyst for the industrial method.

name: Hydrogen meets fluorine
player_sees: gas HF; F2(g) very pale yellow goes; note: Explodes even in the dark and cold; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Halogen'
claim_or_entries: 'A fluorine-hydrogen reaction is explosive even when it is dark and cold', H2 + X2 -> 2HX.

name: Contact process
player_sees: gas SO3; condensation; note: Inside the converter there is nothing to see; on cool glass the sulfur trioxide condenses, and it fumes white in moist air; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Contact process'
claim_or_entries: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g), dH = -197 kJ/mol, at 420-620 C over vanadium(V) oxide.

name: Sulfuric acid forms
player_sees: mist of H2SO4 (white); note: Sulfur trioxide meets water violently, making a fog of sulfuric acid droplets; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Contact process'
claim_or_entries: Dissolving SO3 directly in water is 'highly exothermic'; 'acidic vapor or mists are formed instead of a liquid'.
note: The page does not print SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4.

name: Ostwald process, step 1
player_sees: glows; gas NO; gas H2O; condensation; note: The platinum catalyst gauze stays red-hot by itself once started; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ostwald process'
claim_or_entries: 4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O (dH = -905.2 kJ/mol) over platinum gauze at about 900 C; strongly exothermic.

name: Nitric oxide turns brown
player_sees: gas NO2, red-brown; NO2(g) red-brown appears; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ostwald process'
claim_or_entries: 2NO + O2 -> 2NO2 (dH = -114.2 kJ/mol); Wikipedia 'Nitric oxide': nitrogen dioxide is a brown gas.

name: Nitric acid forms
player_sees: gas NO; NO2(g) red-brown goes; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ostwald process'
claim_or_entries: 3NO2 + H2O -> 2HNO3 + NO (dH = -117 kJ/mol).

name: Lightning fixes nitrogen
player_sees: gas NO; note: Nothing to see at first: nitric oxide is colourless (it turns brown later in air); takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Nitric oxide'
claim_or_entries: 'The uncatalyzed endothermic reaction of oxygen and nitrogen' at over 2000 C 'by lightning': N2 + O2 -> 2NO; NO is colourless.

name: Steam reforming
player_sees: gas CO; gas H2; note: Nothing to see: colourless gases; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Steam reforming'
claim_or_entries: Methane and steam over a nickel catalyst at 800-900 C; 'strongly endothermic (206 kJ/mol)'.
note: The equation itself did not render on the page.

name: Water-gas shift
player_sees: gas CO2; gas H2; note: Nothing to see: colourless gases; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Water-gas shift reaction'
claim_or_entries: CO + H2O <=> CO2 + H2, dH = -41.2 kJ/mol, over iron-chromium or copper catalysts.

name: Water gas
player_sees: glows; gas CO; gas H2; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Water gas'
claim_or_entries: H2O + C -> H2 + CO (dH = +131 kJ/mol), steam over red-hot coke.

name: Boudouard reaction
player_sees: glows; gas CO; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Boudouard reaction'
claim_or_entries: 2CO <=> CO2 + C is exothermic, so CO2 + C -> 2CO takes in heat and is favoured at high temperature.

name: Methanol synthesis
player_sees: gas CH3OH; condensation; note: Inside the plant there is nothing to see; on cool glass the methanol vapour condenses to colourless droplets; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Methanol'
claim_or_entries: CO + 2H2 -> CH3OH at 5-10 MPa and 250 C over copper and zinc oxides.

name: Making urea
player_sees: gas H2O; condensation; note: White urea comes out of a colourless melt; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Urea'
claim_or_entries: Urea is made from ammonia and carbon dioxide: 2NH3 + CO2 <=> NH4CO2NH2, then NH4CO2NH2 <=> CO(NH2)2 + H2O; the overall conversion is exothermic; urea is a white solid.
note: The game writes the two steps as one.

name: Limestone roasts
player_sees: glows; gas CO2; takes in heat
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.1 'Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations'
claim_or_entries: Gives CaCO3(s) -(heat)-> CaO(s) + CO2(g); Wikipedia 'Calcium oxide': quicklime heated strongly glows (limelight).

name: Quicklime meets water
player_sees: condensation; note: The lumps hiss, swell and crumble; the heat boils some of the water into steam; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Calcium oxide'
claim_or_entries: CaO(s) + H2O(l) <=> Ca(OH)2 (dH = -63.7 kJ per mole of CaO); 'the solid puffs up'.

name: Slaked lime dries out
player_sees: gas H2O; condensation; note: Water vapour comes off and condenses on cool glass; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Calcium oxide'
claim_or_entries: 'The hydrate can be reconverted to quicklime by removing the water', by heating it to redness.

name: Copper carbonate turns black
player_sees: gas CO2; CuCO3(s) green goes; CuO(s) black appears; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Basic copper carbonate'
claim_or_entries: The green solid decomposes on heating into H2O, CO2 and CuO (black); true CuCO3 is rarely met, and 'copper carbonate' usually means the basic carbonate.
note: Simplified: the game writes CuCO3 for the basic carbonate Cu2(OH)2CO3, as school textbooks do, and leaves out the water.

name: Magnesium carbonate roasts
player_sees: gas CO2; note: Little to see: one white powder becomes another as the gas leaves; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Magnesium carbonate'
claim_or_entries: 'At high temperatures MgCO3 decomposes to magnesium oxide and carbon dioxide.'

name: Baking soda in the oven
player_sees: gas H2O; gas CO2; condensation; note: Water droplets condense at the cool end of the tube; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Sodium bicarbonate'
claim_or_entries: Gives 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2, 'an endothermic reaction'.

name: Potassium chlorate gives oxygen
player_sees: gas O2; note: With manganese dioxide as the catalyst, oxygen comes off the hot powder below the chlorate's melting point; a glowing splint held in it relights; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Potassium chlorate'
claim_or_entries: Gives 2KClO3(s) + MnO2(cat) -> 3O2(g) + 2KCl(s) when heated.
note: That it gives out heat is from CRC enthalpies of formation (-77.6 kJ), not from the page.

name: Mercury oxide splits
player_sees: gas Hg; gas O2; HgO(s) red goes; Hg(l) silvery appears; condensation; note: The red powder darkens and disappears as silvery droplets of mercury collect on the cool glass. Mercury vapour is poisonous: schools no longer do this, and it is shown on video only; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Mercury(II) oxide'
claim_or_entries: Above 500 C, 'heating produces highly toxic mercury fumes and oxygen'; HgO is red or orange; Priestley found oxygen this way in 1774.

name: Silver oxide splits
player_sees: gas O2; Ag2O(s) brown-black goes; Ag(s) shiny silver appears; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Silver oxide'
claim_or_entries: A black or dark brown powder that reduces to metallic silver above about 380 C.
note: The page does not name oxygen as the other product.

name: Copper nitrate roasts

player_sees: solid CaCO3 (white); little heat change
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2, Table 4.1 'Solubilities of Common Ionic Compounds in Water'

name: White precipitate
player_sees: solid Mg(OH)2 (white); little heat change
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2, Table 4.1 'Solubilities of Common Ionic Compounds in Water'

name: Lead chloride settles
player_sees: solid PbCl2 (white); little heat change
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2, Table 4.1 'Solubilities of Common Ionic Compounds in Water'

note: PbCl2 is fairly soluble (about 10 g/L): it comes out only from fairly concentrated solutions.

name: Zinc hydroxide forms
player_sees: solid Zn(OH)2 (white); gives off heat; feels: It barely warms the mixture: well under a degree with 0.1 M solutions.
source: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2, Table 4.1 'Solubilities of Common Ionic Compounds in Water'

name: Fizzy water
player_sees: note: Under pressure the gas dissolves and you see nothing; open the bottle and it fizzes out again. An indicator would show the water turning slightly acidic; little heat change
source: Wikipedia, 'Carbon dioxide'
claim_or_entries: CO2 + H2O <=> H2CO3: it 'reversibly forms H2CO3 (carbonic acid), which is a weak acid'.

name: Acid rain starts
player_sees: note: Nothing to see: the gas dissolves into an acidic solution; gives off heat; feels: Dissolving a little of the gas barely warms the water.
source: Wikipedia, 'Sulfur dioxide'
claim_or_entries: SO2 dissolves to give 'sulfurous acid', which 'cannot be isolated': SO2 + H2O <=> HSO3- + H+.
note: The game writes H2SO3, the usual textbook form.

name: Ammonia in water
player_sees: note: Nothing to see: the gas dissolves very readily and the water warms; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ammonia'
claim_or_entries: 'Ammonia readily dissolves in water'; the solution 'may be described as aqueous ammonia or ammonium hydroxide'.
note: The game writes NH4OH; the page does not say dissolving warms the water.

name: Sodium oxide meets water
player_sees: note: The white solid dissolves and the water warms; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Sodium oxide'
claim_or_entries: Gives Na2O + H2O -> 2NaOH, readily and irreversibly.

name: Phosphoric acid forms
player_sees: note: The white powder hisses as it dissolves; the water gets hot; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Phosphorus pentoxide'
claim_or_entries: Gives P4O10 + 6H2O -> 4H3PO4 (-177 kJ), exothermic.

name: Hydrogenation
player_sees: gas C2H6; note: Nothing to see: colourless gases; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Hydrogenation'
claim_or_entries: Alkenes add hydrogen to give alkanes over nickel, palladium or platinum; heats of hydrogenation of alkenes are -90 to -130 kJ/mol.
note: General alkene reaction applied to ethene.

name: Bromine water test
player_sees: Br2(aq) yellow-orange goes; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, '1,2-Dibromoethane'
claim_or_entries: Gives CH2=CH2 + Br2 -> BrCH2-CH2Br; Wikipedia 'Bromine': 'alkenes turn brown aqueous bromine solutions colourless'.

name: Ethanol from ethene
player_sees: gas C2H5OH; condensation; note: Nothing to see: colourless gases and vapour; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ethylene'
claim_or_entries: Direct hydration over solid acid catalysts: C2H4 + H2O -> CH3CH2OH; Wikipedia 'Ethanol': with steam at 300 C over phosphoric acid.

name: Making a fruity ester
player_sees: note: A fruity smell; the liquids stay colourless; little heat change
source: Wikipedia, 'Ethanol'
claim_or_entries: 'In the presence of acid catalysts, ethanol reacts with carboxylic acids to produce ethyl esters and water.'
note: General statement; acetic acid and ethyl acetate are not named.

name: Methane meets chlorine
player_sees: gas CH3Cl; gas HCl; Cl2(g) pale yellow-green goes; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Chloromethane'
claim_or_entries: Methane and chlorine at elevated temperature: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl, with more highly chlorinated by-products.
note: The game uses light as the condition; the page names heat.

name: Ethanol loses water
player_sees: gas C2H4; gas H2O; condensation; note: Colourless gas comes off; nothing else to see; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ethanol'
claim_or_entries: CH3CH2OH -> H2C=CH2 + H2O, at high temperature with an acid catalyst.

name: Cracking oil
player_sees: gas C8H18; gas C2H4; condensation; note: Colourless vapour over the hot catalyst; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Cracking (chemistry)'
claim_or_entries: Cracking breaks long alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes such as ethene over silica-alumina or zeolite catalysts; it is endothermic.
note: General process; decane -> octane + ethene is the usual textbook example, not on the page.

name: Sugar splits in two
player_sees: note: Nothing to see: the sugar solution stays clear; little heat change
source: Wikipedia, 'Inverted sugar syrup'
claim_or_entries: C12H22O11 + H2O -> C6H12O6 (glucose) + C6H12O6 (fructose), catalysed by acid or invertase.

name: Ozone forms
player_sees: gas O3; note: Nothing to see: ozone is colourless at this strength, but it has a sharp smell; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ozone'
claim_or_entries: 'Ozone may be formed from O2 by electrical discharges'; colourless or pale blue, with a sharp smell.
note: The page does not print 3O2 -> 2O3 or its heat.

name: Ozone splits
player_sees: gas O2; note: Nothing to see: colourless gases; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ozone'
claim_or_entries: 2O3 -> 3O2; ultraviolet light decomposes ozone.

name: Brown gas pales
player_sees: gas N2O4; NO2(g) red-brown goes; note: The brown gas fades as it cools; warming brings the colour back; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Ostwald process'
claim_or_entries: 2NO2 -> N2O4 (dH = -57.2 kJ/mol).

name: Making glass
player_sees: glows; gas CO2; note: Carbon dioxide bubbles up through the glowing melt; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Sodium silicate'
claim_or_entries: x Na2CO3 + SiO2 -> (Na2O)x.SiO2 + x CO2 with the carbonate molten (x = 1 here).

name: Lime meets sand
player_sees: glows; gas CO2; takes in heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Wollastonite'
claim_or_entries: Gives CaCO3 + SiO2 -> CaSiO3 + CO2.
note: The page describes it at high temperature and pressure in rocks; the game's say line notes that real cement clinker is richer in calcium.

name: Touch powder
player_sees: gas N2; gas I2, violet; vapour of I2 (violet); note: Touching the dry solid sets off a sharp crack and a puff of violet iodine vapour; gives off heat
source: Wikipedia, 'Nitrogen triiodide'
claim_or_entries: 2NI3(s) -> N2(g) + 3I2(g) (-290 kJ/mol), an extremely sensitive contact explosive 'releasing a purple cloud of iodine vapor'.
note: The real solid is the ammonia adduct NI3.NH3.
